text: Dev Log #1: I'm building a web browser for a G3 iMac from 1999 running Mac OS 9. Not as a joke. Real HTTPS, real CSS, real JavaScript. It loads actual websites from 1999 hardware. That's the whole premise. It works. https://macsurf.org

Dev Log #2: The compiler is CodeWarrior 8. It only understands C89 — no `inline`, no `//` comments, no 64-bit math that actually works. Building a modern browser in a 1989 language spec. You stop fighting the constraints and start building around them. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #3: OS 9 has no preemptive threading. The whole OS runs cooperative — one thing runs at a time, you yield by hand. No background fetch threads. Every network request has to give back control manually. You think differently about code. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #4: We shipped native TLS 1.3 on Classic Mac OS. First time ever. X25519 key exchange, ChaCha20-Poly1305, the full Mozilla CA bundle baked in. On a G3 iMac. No proxy, no cheat — the Mac is the real client. https://macsurf.org

Dev Log #5: Porting libcss to CodeWarrior 8 was 303 .c files. Every inline had to go. Every // comment. Every C99 designated initializer. One file had 47 of them. You count by hand, fix one by one, and eventually the cascade parses. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

OS 9 History: Mac OS 9 shipped in October 1999. The web that year was tables, frames, and Netscape 4. The G3 iMac was the hot consumer machine. Nobody was thinking about what would happen to these computers 25 years later.

Dev Log #6: CodeWarrior 8 has a compiler bug. `(long long)a * constant` silently writes the wrong value to the high word. It compiles. It links. CSS layout breaks in ways that look like logic errors. You find it by probing the math at the machine level. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #7: Every Carbon app on OS 9 needs a `'carb'` resource in its resource fork or it crashes inside OTClientLib at a fixed address. Not a useful error. Just a crash. The resource is a two-byte marker that tells CFM the binary is Carbon. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #8: QuickDraw `CopyBits` colorizes the image toward the port's current foreground color. After drawing blue link text, every image blit was blue-tinted. Not obviously — just faded and wrong. It looked like a decoder bug. It was two lines of fix. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #9: CSS custom properties (`var()`) work natively on the G3. The lexer was splitting `--foo` into two tokens because the CSS 2.1 grammar only had one leading dash. One branch added to the lexer state machine. 219 `var()` references start resolving. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #10: Duktape 2.7.0 runs on the G3. Full ES5 — closures, prototypes, regex, JSON, promises, recursion. On a PowerPC chip with 64MB of RAM. It compiled on CodeWarrior 8 with zero patches to the engine source. Only config changes. https://macsurf.org

OS 9 History: Internet Explorer 5 for Mac was genuinely good. Shipped in 2000, supported real CSS, had a working JS engine, passed standards tests IE for Windows couldn't touch. Microsoft killed it in 2003 and never replaced it. Classic Mac users had nothing.

Dev Log #11: Modern sites use ES6. Duktape speaks ES5. So I wrote a transpiler in C89 that rewrites ES6 to ES5 on the fly when Duktape throws a SyntaxError. Runs on the Mac itself. No proxy, no server-side step. The Mac does the work. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #12: ES6 `for...of` loops don't exist in ES5. The transpiler catches them and converts to indexed for loops — handling nested loops, multiple iterators, break/continue. The edge cases are where the real work is. It runs in C89. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #13: ES6 arrow functions: `(x) => x + 1`. The transpiler rewrites them as `function(x) { return x + 1; }` with correct `this` binding via a closure. Handles nested arrows. Works in a single pass before Duktape sees the source. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #14: Template literals: `hello ${name}` converted to string concatenation. Sounds simple. Nested expressions, escaped backticks, multi-line strings — those are the failure modes. Handled in a single-pass C89 scanner. On a G3. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #15: Facebook serves a 416KB JavaScript SPA if you show up with a modern browser UA. We spoof an IE5 Mac UA. Facebook redirects to mbasic.facebook.com — pure HTML, no JS, ~6KB per page. It renders on the G3. https://macsurf.org

OS 9 History: At WWDC 2002, Steve Jobs walked out to a funeral dirge and showed a tombstone on screen that said "Mac OS 9." He declared it dead. No more development. The crowd laughed. The people who still depended on OS 9 hardware did not.

Dev Log #16: NetSurf's cookie jar existed in the codebase but was only wired to the curl fetcher, which we don't build. Our fetchers sent no Cookie header and stored no Set-Cookie. Login was just broken. Three lines of code fixed it. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #17: First real non-Facebook login: 68kmla.org, a vintage Mac forum running phpBB. Typed the credentials, hit submit, got the session cookie, stayed logged in across pages. The whole auth stack — form POST, cookies, redirect — worked. https://macsurf.org

Dev Log #18: Facebook's full site was returning 400. Spent a while suspecting TLS issues, HTTP/2 requirements. The actual problem: we weren't sending Sec-Fetch-Dest, Sec-Fetch-Mode, Sec-Fetch-Site. Four headers. That was it. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #19: The scroll wheel crashes MacSurf on real G3 hardware. kEventMouseWheelMoved is marked "CarbonLib: not available" in Apple's own header. We installed a handler anyway. CarbonLib's dispatcher walked uninitialized state and died. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #20: Scroll bar live tracking with proc 386 crashed on real G3 hardware but not in emulation. SheepShaver's CarbonLib tolerates the same call that real hardware rejects. Switched to proc 384. Crash gone. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

OS 9 History: Classilla was the last real browser for Classic Mac OS — a port of Mozilla 1.3, maintained by one person (Cameron Kaiser) for years after Apple walked away. Kept alive by sheer stubbornness. MacSurf exists in that same tradition. https://macsurf.org

Dev Log #21: Overriding NewControlActionUPP to a raw function pointer works on macOS Mach-O. On CarbonLib it goes through MixedMode, reads garbage from the function entry bytes, executes `bl 0`. PC lands at 0x00000008. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #22: We had a hard crash at 0x2710 after page loads. Assumed use-after-free. It was heap and stack exhaustion — two full box trees in RAM plus deep JS-DOM recursion on a 10MB page. Bumped the Carbon partition. Crash gone. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #23: Every hover event was triggering a full CSS recascade of the entire page. On first real-world use — mbasic Facebook, 160 boxes — this leaked styles on every hover until the heap was gone. The Mac crashed in garbage memory. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #24: The ICO favicon handler called content_set_done() AND returned true. NetSurf fires DONE on both. On a machine with no memory protection, that's a whole-machine crash. The bug lived there silently for months. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #25: XenForo forums use a 12-column CSS Grid. Our grid engine had a hard cap of 16 tracks — fine for most sites. But some column placements were starting at index 13 and collapsing the layout. Upgraded the cap to 32. Sites load. https://macsurf.org

OS 9 History: The G3 iMac shipped in 1998 — translucent plastic, five colors, no floppy drive. It was a cultural moment. Apple was nearly bankrupt, Steve Jobs had just returned, and this machine turned it around. It was never supposed to run anything from 2026.

Dev Log #26: The debug log writes to "MacSurf Debug.log" on the Desktop and flushes after every line with FlushVol. When the Mac crashes — and it will — the last line in the log is the last thing that ran. It's saved dozens of hours. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #27: The render engine clips boxes with obviously garbage coordinates. Original threshold: +/-10,000 pixels. When the test page grew past 10,000 pixels tall, it clipped the valid root box to zero. Page rendered blank. Raised to +/-200,000. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #28: Font rendering on OS 9.1 looks rougher than on 9.2.2 — same code, same settings. Apple improved QuickDraw's AA path in 9.2. SetAntiAliasedTextEnabled just doesn't respond as well on 9.1 above 8pt. OS limit, not a bug. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #29: #include <Carbon.h> on CW8 chains into InternetConfig.h, which uses AliasRecord before Aliases.h loads. Including Aliases.h first re-enters Carbon.h. Fix: predefine __INTERNETCONFIG__ before the include. Carbon.h skips the file. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #30: SheepShaver runs OS 9.0.4 and MacSurf launches fine — Carbon init, UI, rendering. But its CarbonLib is more forgiving than real hardware, and it can't do real network requests. Green in emulation doesn't mean green on a G3. https://macsurf.org

OS 9 History: Mac OS 9's cooperative multitasking was already ancient when it shipped in 1999. Windows NT had preemptive threading. BeOS had it. Linux had it. Apple shipped OS 9 knowing OS X was the real future. OS 9 was a bridge nobody wanted to stay on.

Dev Log #31: BearSSL is a TLS library designed for embedded systems. Porting it to PPC Mac OS 9 meant verifying every 32-bit multiply was correct on CW8. Then building the full TLS 1.3 handshake around it. It works. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #32: X25519 Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman runs on a G3. No hardware acceleration. Pure C arithmetic on a PPC chip from 1998. Handshake completes. The forward secrecy is real. The math is just the math. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #33: macEntropy is the RNG we built for the TLS stack. OS 9 has no /dev/random. We seed from mouse position, tick count, memory state, process timing — everything that varies between runs. TLS without a good RNG is not TLS. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #34: TLS session resumption: after a first connection, the handshake state is cached. Next connection skips the key exchange. Verified against 68kmla.org — binder accepted, cert verify skipped, app data over resumed keys. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #35: HKDF expand: br_hmac_out always writes the full hash length. Sub-digest outputs like 12-byte IVs, pointed at a 12-byte buffer, overflow into adjacent key material. Fix: scratch buffer, then memcpy. A completed handshake is NOT proof the keys are right. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

OS 9 History: The Power Mac G4 was sold in 2001 as a "supercomputer." Apple filed an export control challenge because the G4 exceeded the FLOPS threshold for classified weapons technology. You couldn't legally export one to certain countries. Now it runs MacSurf. https://macsurf.org

Dev Log #36: The image fetcher had no memory safety on large files. Loading a high-res JPEG would try to decode a multi-MB bitmap into a 64MB heap that's already half full. Added a 512KB abort threshold. Heap crashes dropped to zero. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #37: PNG alpha transparency on Classic QuickDraw: QTNewGWorld with 32-bit ARGB format returns error -157 on OS 9. That pixel format is QuickTime 6 / Mach-O only. So we implemented alpha compositing ourselves in a 32-bit GWorld. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #38: After every image decode, the source data buffer was sitting in the cache. For a session loading dozens of images, this added up fast. One line: free the source buffer after decode. The heap stays clean. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #39: We abort HTTP downloads over 512KB to protect the heap. The abort was only wired on the HTTPS side. On plain HTTP, large downloads still crashed. Found it the hard way. Now both fetchers gate on the same threshold. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #40: Chunked transfer encoding: the server sends data with a hex length prefix, you read that many bytes, read the CRLF, repeat until the zero-length chunk. Implemented in C89 over Open Transport. Works on OS 9. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

OS 9 History: Mac OS 9.2.2 shipped in December 2001. It was the last release of Classic Mac OS. Apple never announced it as the final version — no ceremony, no press release. It just stopped. The OS 9 era ended quietly while everyone was looking at OS X.

Dev Log #41: HTTP keep-alive — reuse the TCP connection for the next request instead of tearing it down. On OS 9 with Open Transport, managing the pool means tracking state across cooperative yields by hand. Saves a lot of round trips. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #42: OTInitDNSAddress — one call, Open Transport resolves the hostname and port together. Compared to: resolve IP, create an inet address struct, fill in the port separately. Small API detail. The difference is readable code. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #43: When Open Transport blocks on a synchronous call, it fires kOTSyncIdleEvent. We respond by calling YieldToAnyThread(). The app stays cooperative without touching the event loop from inside the fetch. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #44: Every NetSurf fetcher must call both fetch_remove_from_queues() AND fetch_free() after a terminal callback. Call only fetch_free() and the handle stays in the ring as a dangling pointer. The next ring walk reads freed memory. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #45: Aborted-while-queued fetches: if the abort flag isn't checked before the state-based early-return, aborted fetches stay in the ring forever. Symptom: browser stops after about three pages. The abort check has to come first. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

OS 9 History: iCab was a German-made browser for Classic Mac OS that outlasted everything else. Small, fast, and it had a smiley face in the toolbar that turned sad when the page had invalid HTML. Ahead of its time and trapped on a platform nobody was updating.

Dev Log #46: Without the 'carb' resource, CFM treats the binary as classic PEF. CarbonLib doesn't load as a dependency. Any InContext Open Transport call enters an uninitialized context and crashes. One 2-byte resource fixes all of it. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #47: CSS Grid on OS 9: track sizing, fr units, gap, column/row spans, explicit placement. libcss parses the declarations, our layout engine distributes the tracks. XenForo, news sites, documentation — all render correctly. https://macsurf.org

Dev Log #48: CSS Flexbox: main axis, cross axis, wrapping, alignment, gap. Ported to C89 and wired into the NetSurf layout engine on a G3. flex-direction, justify-content, align-items. Modern layout primitives running on 1999 hardware. https://macsurf.org

Dev Log #49: CSS transforms on OS 9: translate(), scale(), rotate(). QuickDraw doesn't support matrix transforms natively. We apply them at paint time using fixed-point math, carefully working around the int64 miscompile bug in CW8. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #50: border-radius and box-shadow both work. border-radius is clipped using QuickDraw region intersection. box-shadow draws a blurred rect behind the element. Neither was in the original NetSurf codebase for OS 9. We wrote it. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

OS 9 History: The Carbon API was Apple's bridge — write Carbon C code, it runs on OS 9 AND OS X. Designed to give developers a migration path without a full rewrite. MacSurf uses Carbon. The same binary could theoretically run on early OS X. https://macsurf.org

Dev Log #51: CSS gradients — linear and radial — render on the G3. We rasterize the gradient into a GWorld pixel by pixel at layout time, then blit it. Slow for very large elements, but for typical card backgrounds: fast enough. https://macsurf.org

Dev Log #52: PNG, JPEG, GIF, BMP, TIFF — all five image handlers work on OS 9. Each decodes to a GWorld, composites alpha if present, hands the bitmap to the layout engine. Images load on real websites. This was a long road. https://macsurf.org

Dev Log #53: libdom is 95 .c files — the DOM implementation. Every file had to be C89 clean. Tracking down designated initializers, inline keywords, and C99 variable-in-for across 95 files took weeks. Now the HTML parser has a real DOM to build into. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #54: libhubbub is the HTML5 parser — 30 .c files, a hand-written state machine that handles malformed HTML the same way modern browsers do. Porting it to CW8 C89 meant converting everything CW8 doesn't understand. It parses everything. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #55: The address bar prepends http:// if you don't type a scheme. Routes through nsurl_create for full URL normalization — percent encoding, path canonicalization, scheme lowercasing. Sounds boring. It's load-bearing. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

OS 9 History: Netscape 4 for Mac OS 9 was the dominant browser in 1999. It supported CSS 1 poorly, crashed constantly, and the entire web was coded around its bugs. When Netscape 4 died, the web got better. OS 9 users had nothing left.

Dev Log #56: TENew (TextEdit) crashes with a memory error if SetWRefCon hasn't been called on the window first. GetWRefCon returns garbage on a fresh window. TextEdit dereferences it. The fix is two lines before TENew. Three days to find. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #57: We renamed dispatch.c to s_dispatch.c to avoid a symbol clash in CW8's flat namespace. A later commit re-added a stale dispatch.c. Shipping updates only to dispatch.c was invisible to the build. Both files have to stay in sync. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #58: New fields in css_computed_style_i must go at the end. Adding one in the middle shifts every field after it. CW8 misses the recompile sometimes. Old .o files link fine. At runtime the layout engine reads the wrong offsets and crashes. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #59: row-gap and column-gap share the same storage slot in our libcss port. gap: 20px 40px silently loses the first value. Both axes get 40px. Fixing it properly requires a new CSS property enum and a bit-packing audit. Deferred. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #60: In CW8 PPC, int32_t is long, not int. int* and long* are incompatible types and CW8 is strict about it. Autogenerated libcss files had int* ctx where the rest of the codebase used int32_t* ctx. Hard error, not a warning. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

OS 9 History: HFS+ shipped with Mac OS 8.1 in 1998. The original HFS had a file limit per volume so low that a large hard drive wasted enormous space in allocation blocks. HFS+ was Apple's filesystem until APFS in 2017. The Mac running MacSurf still uses it.

Dev Log #61: C89 forbids casting to union types. (css_fixed_or_calc)0 — readable code — is a hard error in CW8. Fix: declare a local variable of the union type, assign the field, pass it. More words. Same meaning. Compiles. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #62: Forward enum declarations (enum foo;) are illegal in C89. A C99 header used one to break a circular include. The fix was to include the full header earlier in the chain. CW8 gives you no grace period — it just fails. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #63: plotters.c used to find the current window by calling GetPort() and casting to WindowRef. Works fine until any code calls SetGWorld(offscreen, NULL). Then the cast reads garbage. Every draw call fired but nothing appeared on screen. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #64: Any new CSS visual property — gradient, shadow, outline — has to register in html_redraw_box_has_background or it silently no-ops when the element has no background-color. It's a gate. You're either in the list or nothing draws. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #65: Originally the scrollbar moved by one text line per click. Wiring in content_get_height() for pixel-based scroll made the bar track actual content position. Pages scroll smoothly now. It was a bigger change than it sounds. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

OS 9 History: The Classic environment in OS X let you run OS 9 apps inside a compatibility layer. Apple removed it entirely in OS X 10.5 Leopard in 2007. After that, if you needed OS 9, you needed actual OS 9 hardware.

Dev Log #66: Early in development the title bar was the only debug output that worked reliably. Function name, hex value, state flag — updated in real time on hardware. We still use it alongside the file-backed log. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #67: NSLOG in NetSurf uses GNU variadic macros. CW8 C89 doesn't officially support them — except it does, as a pre-C99 extension. One correct macro definition. 200+ compile errors gone. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #68: CW8 fails to complete a struct that has a named enum declared inside it. Anonymous enums inside structs work fine. Named ones leave the struct incomplete. Hoisting the enum before the struct definition fixes it. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #69: Shim headers that claim the real header's include guard but don't define the types silently block the real header. CW8 finds the shim first, sets the guard, then skips the real header. Incomplete type errors on structs the shim never declared. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #70: The CW8 access path puts our shim html/html.h before the real one. If the shim sets the real guard without defining struct html_script, every file that includes it gets an empty substitution. The shim must forward to the real header. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

OS 9 History: The Appearance Manager in Mac OS 8/9 introduced themes to the Classic Mac UI. The Platinum look — that gray, beveled, tactile chrome — defined late-90s Macs. MacSurf's window lives inside that same Platinum chrome. https://macsurf.org

Dev Log #71: MacSurf.mcp has ~470 .c files. libcss alone is 303. libdom is 95. libhubbub is 30. libparserutils is 15. Plus 12 frontend files, 5 shims, 10 NetSurf core files. Every one was audited for C89 compliance and ported by hand. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #72: Target hardware: G3 iMac, Mac OS 9.2.2, 64MB RAM. That 64MB includes the OS, the browser binary, the render tree, all decoded images, the JavaScript heap, and the TLS state. Every allocation decision matters. There is no swap space. https://macsurf.org

Dev Log #73: Cooperative multitasking teaches you that yield points are a first-class design decision. Every blocking operation has to hand back control explicitly. Once you internalize that, the code gets cleaner — because the cost is visible. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #74: The architecture: HTTP and HTTPS fetch directly from the Mac to the origin. No proxy. The TLS stack is native C linked into the binary. CSS via a port of libcss. HTML via libhubbub. JS via Duktape. All on the G3. https://macsurf.org

Dev Log #75: mactrove.com was causing 15 full layout reformats per page load — one for every subresource that finished. Each reformat walks the full render tree. Fix: coalesce them, trigger once when the last resource is done. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

OS 9 History: The first iMac G3 revision had no Ethernet — just a modem. Getting online meant dial-up. Later revisions added Ethernet and AirPort. The one running MacSurf has Ethernet. That's how a 1999 machine reaches the real web in 2026. https://macsurf.org

Dev Log #76: The JS probe page tests 19 browser APIs: setTimeout, fetch, localStorage, URL, classList, MutationObserver, DOMParser, FormData, history.pushState, and more. Scores 19/19 on a G3 iMac. All on-device. https://macsurf.org

Dev Log #77: MutationObserver on a G3 iMac running OS 9. We implemented the spec: observe a node, queue the mutations, fire the callback on the next microtask. SPAs use this everywhere. It works. The Mac keeps up. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #78: localStorage.setItem / getItem on Mac OS 9. Backed by a flat file in the preferences folder — serialize to JSON, write to disk, parse on next launch. Sites that depend on local state work across sessions. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #79: fetch() as a browser API — returns a Promise, resolves with a Response, .json(), .text(). Wired to our real HTTP and HTTPS fetchers. Sites that use fetch instead of XMLHttpRequest just work. On a G3. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

Dev Log #80: new URL('https://example.com/path?q=1') parses correctly. URLSearchParams.get('q') returns '1'. ES2015 globals that sites use constantly. Implemented in C89 glue code wired to Duktape. Small surface area, big compat gain. https://github.com/mplsllc/macsurf

OS 9 History: The web was built assuming you had Windows. The Mac IE team had to fight to get CSS support taken seriously. When Microsoft shut down Mac IE in 2003, the message was clear: the web was moving on and old hardware wasn't invited.

Dev Story #1: The first JavaScript output on Classic Mac OS was "Hello from Duktape on Mac OS 9!" on April 15, 2026. A G3 iMac from 1998. Then it drew an ASCII Mandelbrot fractal. It had never been done before on this platform. https://macsurf.org

Dev Story #2: The G3 where a lot of early MacSurf work happened belonged to Gary Hansen, who passed away. His machine — with his own processor upgrade still installed — was still compiling code and rendering fractals in 2026. This project is dedicated to his memory. https://macsurf.org

Dev Story #3: I started this because I wanted to see how far you could push a machine that "can't" do something. The G3 iMac can't browse the modern web. Now it does. The question was never whether — it was always how. https://macsurf.org

Dev Story #4: There's something archaeological about this work. Digging through code from the 90s, figuring out what the designers were optimizing for, working out which constraints were real and which were assumptions. Not restoration. Excavation. https://macsurf.org

Dev Story #5: The design goal was always: the Mac is the real client. No proxy to strip TLS, no server-side JS processing, no helper app to handle the hard parts. The G3 reaches the internet on its own. That's the whole point. https://macsurf.org

Dev Story #6: When you can't throw more hardware at a problem, you have to understand the problem. Every byte in 64MB is intentional. Every yield point in the event loop is designed. Constraints don't limit the project. They define it. https://macsurf.org

Dev Story #7: Modern browsers are millions of lines of code because they've accumulated decades of compatibility shims and features nobody uses. This project is the opposite: what's the minimum needed to actually load a webpage? It's still a lot. But a known lot. https://macsurf.org

Dev Story #8: The moment native HTTPS worked on the G3 — certificate verified, keys exchanged, actual data decrypted on the machine itself — that was the landmark. First native TLS 1.3 on Classic Mac OS. It wasn't fast. It didn't matter. https://macsurf.org

Dev Story #9: We loaded Facebook on a G3 iMac. Not a screenshot, not a proxy pass-through. The Mac negotiated the connection, sent the request with our cookies, got back HTML, rendered it. My actual Facebook content. On a machine from 1999. https://macsurf.org
